lane.name: Dylan and The Band
lane.definition: Bob Dylan from going electric through the Rolling Thunder era and The Band's catalog: the model for roots-conscious rock songwriting.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Dylan splits the record down the middle: one side of a loud electric band driving surreal, joke-cracking talking blues, one side of solo acoustic guitar and harmonica carrying his most abstract lyrics yet. It is the record where folk-club Dylan becomes rock Dylan without fully leaving either behind, and it set the template for treating rock lyrics as literature.
albums.lineage: Grows directly out of the Greenwich Village folk revival (Guthrie, Van Ronk) and electric Chicago/Chess blues; its fusion of rock band and literary lyric is the founding document the whole V22 lane, and later Neil Young and The Band, build on.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A full-band electric record built on Mike Bloomfield's guitar and Al Kooper's improvised organ, moving from the six-minute single 'Like a Rolling Stone' to the eleven-minute closing ballad 'Desolation Row'. The songs are dense with carnival imagery, biblical and pop-culture references, sung in a sneering, speed-of-thought delivery that reinvented what a rock lyric could hold.
albums.lineage: Follows directly from Bringing It All Back Home's electric side; later roots-rock songwriters from The Band to Drive-By Truckers sound indebted to its extended narrative-song form.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A double album cut mostly in Nashville with top session players, giving Dylan's wild-mercury wordplay a loose, bluesy backing instead of a garage-rock one. It stretches from the tumbling wordplay of 'Rainy Day Women #12 & 35' to the eleven-minute side-long 'Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands', and its use of Nashville cats previews the country turn to come.
albums.lineage: Extends the electric trilogy begun on Bringing It All Back Home and Highway 61 Revisited; the Nashville sessions directly set up Dylan's later country records and the whole Nashville-adjacent wing of the V zone.
key_tracks: Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Recorded quickly in Nashville after Dylan's motorcycle-accident seclusion, this is a deliberately plain, parable-like record: mostly just guitar, bass and drums behind biblical outlaw ballads. Arriving amid psychedelia's excess, its austerity and Old West/gospel imagery pointed rock songwriting back toward roots music.
albums.lineage: Follows the Basement Tapes sessions with The Band, and sounds like it anticipates Dylan's own country records and the country-rock turn of the Byrds and Gram Parsons.
key_tracks: I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: The debut album by Dylan's former backing band, cut in the same Woodstock, NY orbit as the Basement Tapes and drawing on two Dylan co-writes plus Robbie Robertson originals like 'The Weight'. Its warm, unhurried blend of country, gospel, R&B and rock, with three lead singers trading verses, arrived as a direct rebuke to psychedelia and reoriented a generation of rock musicians toward roots music.
albums.lineage: Grew directly out of The Band's years backing Dylan and the informal Basement Tapes sessions; Eric Clapton has said the record's plainness helped break up Cream, and it is a founding document for Southern rock, country rock and Americana alike.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Dylan's full country album, cut in Nashville with Charlie Daniels and Pete Drake, sung in a warm new croon after he quit smoking. Short, uncomplicated love songs replace his earlier density, and the Johnny Cash duet on 'Girl from the North Country' formalized the bridge between Music Row and rock songwriters.
albums.lineage: Pushes the country move hinted at on John Wesley Harding all the way into Nashville proper, lending weight to the country-rock movement of V21 that the Byrds' Sweetheart of the Rodeo had kicked off the year before.
key_tracks: Tonight I'll Be Staying Here with You

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: Recorded in a converted pool house in Sammy Davis Jr.'s Hollywood Hills home, this self-titled second album is largely Robbie Robertson's songwriting about a South none of the (mostly Canadian) band members were from, sung by Levon Helm, Rick Danko and Richard Manuel in rotation. 'The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down' and 'King Harvest (Has Surely Come)' are dense character studies that made rock lyrics read like short fiction.
albums.lineage: The high-water mark of The Band's own catalog; the Southern storytelling rock of the Allman Brothers and, decades later, Drive-By Truckers' novelistic songwriting sound indebted to it.
key_tracks: The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A quick, warm corrective to Self Portrait, built around Dylan's own piano playing, with a looser, more domestic feel than his '60s records. Songs like 'If Not for You' and 'New Morning' trade prophecy for contentment, sung in a relaxed, husky voice over small-band backing.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a continuation of the plainspoken, domestic mode of John Wesley Harding and the Basement Tapes, and its warmth resembles the singer-songwriter records of V13 and V25.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A sprawling double album of covers, traditional songs and a few originals, cut with Nashville and Woodstock players and drenched in strings and backing choirs; it was savaged on release for being un-Dylanlike and has since been reassessed as a deliberately loose folk-song scrapbook. It sits closer to easy-listening country-pop than anything he had done before.
albums.lineage: An extension of the covers-and-traditionals instinct from the Basement Tapes sessions, and an early model for later artists' 'anti-image' covers records.

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: Recorded on the stage of the Woodstock Playhouse, this third album sounds bouncier than its predecessor but is full of anxious, self-doubting lyrics about performance and fame. Richard Manuel's and Rick Danko's voices carry that unease over rolling piano and Garth Hudson's organ, making it the most nervous-sounding of the early Band records.
albums.lineage: Follows the character-study songwriting of The Band with more autobiographical unease, reflecting the pressure of following two acclaimed records.

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: A patchier fourth album, cut with the band fraying internally, but still yielding the circus-barker opener 'Life Is a Carnival' (with Allen Toussaint horn charts) and a Dylan song, 'When I Paint My Masterpiece', given an accordion-and-mandolin reading. It is generally ranked below the first three records but still carries the group's signature blend of voices.
albums.lineage: Shows the same Woodstock-honed roots-rock voice as the first three Band albums beginning to strain, foreshadowing the covers-driven Moondog Matinee.

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: A live double album from New York's Academy of Music shows over New Year's 1971-72, with Allen Toussaint horn arrangements fleshing out the band's studio catalog into something brassier and more muscular. It is widely regarded as one of the great '70s live rock albums, loose but locked-in, with Garth Hudson's organ and the horns trading space.
albums.lineage: Captures The Band's core studio catalog (Big Pink through Cahoots) in performance, and its horn-driven arrangements anticipate the larger ensemble sound of The Last Waltz.

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: An all-covers fifth album turning the band loose on the '50s and early-'60s R&B and rock and roll records they grew up on, from Clarence 'Frogman' Henry's 'Ain't Got No Home' to a slow-building take on Junior Parker's 'Mystery Train'. It functions as a look at the group's raw material rather than a songwriting statement.
albums.lineage: Shows the R&B and rockabilly roots underneath the group's own original songwriting, the same well the band drew on for its own sound on Music from Big Pink.

albums.label: Asylum
albums.description: Dylan's only studio album backed entirely by The Band, cut fast in a few days before their 1974 reunion tour. It swings between the ragged, loose road-song feel of 'Tough Mama' and the tender 'Forever Young', written for his children, and is the clearest studio document of how Dylan and The Band's sounds fit together.
albums.lineage: Reunites Dylan with the Basement Tapes-era Band and directly sets up the tour that produced Before the Flood; its loose, road-worn feel points toward Blood on the Tracks the following year.

albums.label: Asylum
albums.description: A double live album from Dylan's 1974 arena reunion tour with The Band, reworking '60s classics at a harder, faster, more triumphant pace than the originals, with The Band also performing a handful of songs from their own catalog in the set. It is loud, celebratory rock and roll rather than a nuanced revisit.
albums.lineage: Grew out of the same 1974 reunion that produced the studio album Planet Waves, and stands as the definitive document of Dylan and The Band performing together on a large stage.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Written in the wake of Dylan's marriage coming apart and recorded twice, first sparsely in New York and then partly re-cut with Minneapolis musicians, the finished record mixes both sessions into an album of shifting-tense breakup songs and long narrative ballads. Acoustic guitar, organ and harmonica carry most of it, and it is widely treated as his songwriting peak.
albums.lineage: A return to acoustic, lyric-first songwriting after the full-band Planet Waves, and a record later confessional and narrative songwriters across the V zone often sound indebted to.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Recorded in 1967 around Woodstock, largely in the basement of The Band's rented house ('Big Pink'), then officially released eight years later, this is loose, half-joking, half-mythic Americana cut on cheap tape with no thought of release. Dylan and The Band run through originals, covers and pure nonsense with a homemade, live-in-the-room looseness that later listeners treated as a founding text of roots rock.
albums.lineage: Grew out of Dylan and The Band's convalescence-era sessions before John Wesley Harding; its ramshackle, communal recording ethic feeds The Band's own catalog and resembles later lo-fi/DIY roots recording.

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: The group's first album of new originals in four years, recorded at their own Shangri-La studio in Malibu, with Garth Hudson layering synthesizer textures under otherwise classic Band arrangements. 'Acadian Driftwood' retells the 18th-century expulsion of Acadians from Nova Scotia, and 'It Makes No Difference' is one of Rick Danko's most acclaimed vocal performances.
albums.lineage: A late creative peak that shows the group's original songwriting voice intact after the covers-heavy Moondog Matinee, though it would be their last full album of new material before Islands.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Most songs co-written with theater director Jacques Levy and driven by Scarlet Rivera's violin, this is Dylan at his most theatrical as a storyteller, from the boxing-injustice epic 'Hurricane' to the surreal travelogue 'Isis'. Emmylou Harris sings harmony throughout, tying the record to the country-rock scene next door.
albums.lineage: Follows Blood on the Tracks' narrative songwriting into wider, almost theatrical storytelling, and its Rolling Thunder-era sound feeds directly into the live document Hard Rain and the tour film/album that followed.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A raw, rain-soaked live album drawn from the second leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue, with Dylan's road band tearing into radically rearranged versions of older songs at a rougher, more ragged pace than the studio originals. It captures the tour's traveling-circus energy better than any polish would.
albums.lineage: Documents the second, harder-edged leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue that followed Desire, and its rough rearrangements set a precedent for Dylan's later habit of remaking his catalog live.

albums.label: Arista
albums.description: The Band bassist and singer's first solo album, sporting the same warm, high-lonesome voice he used on 'It Makes No Difference'. It is gentler and more overtly romantic than most of The Band's catalog, with soft keyboards and easy grooves, closer to a singer-songwriter record than a roots-rock one.
albums.lineage: An offshoot of The Band's mid-'70s dispersal into solo projects, sounding close to the Woodstock-scene singer-songwriter records made around it.

albums.label: Capitol
albums.description: A contract-filling collection of outtakes and newly cut tracks, released after The Last Waltz farewell concert to close out the group's Capitol deal. It is a minor entry next to their '68-'75 run, though 'Right as Rain' and a cover of 'Georgia on My Mind' show the band still capable of warmth.
albums.lineage: The last studio album released under The Band's original lineup, issued after their 1976 farewell concert and closing out the catalog covered by this lane.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A bigger, more R&B-inflected sound than anything Dylan had tried before, with horns, female backing vocalists and a road band cut live in the studio. Reviews were mixed at the time, but 'Changing of the Guards' and 'Señor (Tales of Yankee Power)' are now heard as transitional songs pointing toward the gospel records that followed.
albums.lineage: Bridges the Rolling Thunder era to the born-again gospel trilogy that begins with Slow Train Coming the following year.

albums.label: Warner Bros.
albums.description: The triple-LP soundtrack to Martin Scorsese's concert film of The Band's 1976 farewell show, with an enormous guest list (Dylan, Clapton, Van Morrison, Joni Mitchell, Neil Young, Muddy Waters, Ronnie Hawkins, Dr. John) turning the group's last stand into a summary of the roots-rock lineage they helped build. It remains one of the most acclaimed concert films and live albums in rock history.
albums.lineage: Closes The Band's story as a working group and, by assembling so many of their collaborators and influences on one stage, functions as a family tree for the whole roots-rock lineage this lane covers.
key_tracks: The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: The first of Dylan's born-again Christian albums, cut at Muscle Shoals Sound Studio with Mark Knopfler on guitar and a tight, funky Southern-soul backing band. The evangelical lyrics alienated some longtime fans, but 'Gotta Serve Somebody' and 'Precious Angel' land with real groove and conviction, sung in a hard, preacherly growl.
albums.lineage: A hard turn from the loose road-rock of Street-Legal into gospel testimony, directly setting up Saved and Shot of Love as a trilogy.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A secular comeback co-produced with Mark Knopfler and featuring Sly and Robbie's reggae-tinged rhythm section, generally considered Dylan's strongest '80s studio album. 'Jokerman' and 'Sweetheart Like You' pair dense, allusive lyrics with a cleaner, more contemporary sound than his '70s work.
albums.lineage: Closes out Dylan's religious period and re-establishes the dense, image-driven songwriting of his '60s and '70s work in a modern production context.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Produced by Daniel Lanois in New Orleans, this is a swampy, atmospheric comeback after a rough late-'80s stretch, with hushed, spare arrangements built around Lanois's guitar textures. Dylan writes at length about making it in his memoir Chronicles: Volume One, and 'Most of the Time' and 'Man in the Long Black Coat' are among his most quietly devastating later songs.
albums.lineage: The first of two Lanois-produced comeback records (with Time Out of Mind) that reestablished Dylan as a vital songwriter for a new generation of roots-rock artists.
key_tracks: Man in the Long Black Coat

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A second Daniel Lanois collaboration, this time recorded in Miami with a dense, murky, almost swamp-blues production that suits Dylan's weathered, death-haunted late voice. It won the Grammy for Album of the Year and is generally treated as the start of Dylan's late-period renaissance that runs through Rough and Rowdy Ways.
albums.lineage: Continues the Lanois atmosphere of Oh Mercy but with a heavier, more haunted band sound, opening the door to the more traditional, self-produced records ('Love and Theft' onward) that follow.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Self-produced under the pseudonym Jack Frost, this record trades Time Out of Mind's murk for a dry, swinging pastiche of old-time blues, rockabilly and Tin Pan Alley pop, played by Dylan's touring band. The title, lifted from a scholarly book on minstrelsy, signals the record's deliberate collaging of American vernacular music.
albums.lineage: Moves out of the Lanois-produced fog into the leaner, self-produced sound Dylan keeps for the rest of his career, and its blues/swing pastiche is a direct model for Modern Times.

albums.album: The Bootleg Series Vol. 5: Bob Dylan Live 1975, The Rolling Thunder Revue
albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: An official archival release documenting the first, more theatrical leg of the 1975 Rolling Thunder Revue tour, with Scarlet Rivera's violin and a loose troupe of musicians (Joan Baez, Roger McGuinn among them) reworking Dylan's catalog. It is looser and stranger than the contemporaneous Desire studio takes, capturing the tour's carnival atmosphere the way Hard Rain captures its rougher second leg.
albums.lineage: Part of Dylan's ongoing Bootleg Series of archival releases; it fills in the Rolling Thunder era alongside Desire and Hard Rain and is treated as canonical by Dylan scholars and podcasts like Jokermen.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A relaxed, blues- and swing-soaked record that became Dylan's first number-one album in three decades, leaning on his touring band's road-tested feel and lyrics that freely rework older blues and folk verses. 'Workingman's Blues #2' and the closing 'Ain't Talkin'' extend the antique-Americana persona of 'Love and Theft' into a wearier, more elegiac register.
albums.lineage: The middle record of Dylan's 2000s self-produced trilogy alongside 'Love and Theft' and Together Through Life, deepening his late-career habit of channeling pre-rock American song forms.

albums.label: Vanguard
albums.description: Levon Helm's first studio album in 25 years, made with his daughter Amy Helm among the producers after his recovery from throat cancer, working his weathered voice through old-time murder ballads and traditional songs. Its front-porch, acoustic-forward arrangements of fiddle, mandolin and family harmonies grew out of the Midnight Ramble shows at his Woodstock barn. It is for listeners who want The Band's Southern roots with the rock stripped away.
albums.lineage: Draws on the same Southern folk and old-time repertoire The Band mined, filtered through Helm's own Arkansas roots, and it directly set up his Electric Dirt and Ramble at the Ryman period.

albums.label: Dirt Farmer Music / Vanguard
albums.description: A plugged-in follow-up to Dirt Farmer, adding horns, funk and New Orleans second-line grooves to Helm's old-time base, with covers of the Grateful Dead's 'Tennessee Jed' and Muddy Waters' 'You Can't Lose What You Ain't Never Had' sitting alongside gospel numbers. It won the first Grammy for Best Americana Album.
albums.lineage: Widens the acoustic Dirt Farmer sound into the full electric, horn-driven Band-style roots rock Helm helped invent, his last studio album before his 2012 death.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: A dark, violent late album closing with two extended narrative set-pieces: the fourteen-minute title track retelling the Titanic sinking, and 'Roll On John', an elegy for John Lennon. The touring band plays with a loose, bar-band swing under lyrics that are among Dylan's bleakest.
albums.lineage: Continues the antique-blues persona of 'Love and Theft' and Modern Times toward longer, more explicitly mortality-obsessed narrative songs, setting up Rough and Rowdy Ways.

albums.label: Columbia
albums.description: Dylan's first album of original songs in eight years, anchored by the seventeen-minute 'Murder Most Foul', a stream-of-consciousness meditation on the Kennedy assassination and American culture. Reviewers treated it as a career-capping late masterpiece, direct and plainspoken in a way that contrasts with the riddling density of his '60s work.
albums.lineage: The culmination of the self-produced late style begun on 'Love and Theft', and a record much of the 2020s Americana and indie-folk scene sounds like it treats as a living reference point.
